sections.overview: The muskrat is a medium-sized rodent of fresh and brackish wetlands, with an insulating coat and aquatic adaptations for foraging among emergent plants and retreating to shelters with underwater entrances. Native to North America, it has also established introduced populations across parts of Europe and Asia.
sections.identification: Adults have a head-and-body length of about 23–33 cm, a tail 18–30 cm, and a mass of roughly 0.7–1.9 kg; size varies among populations. The tail is nearly naked, scaly and compressed from side to side, about as long as the head and body. Stiff hairs fringe the toes, and the hind toes are partly webbed; small ears sit almost hidden in dense brown fur. Unlike the much larger beaver, it has a narrow, laterally flattened tail; nutria are far heavier and have a rounded tail with conspicuous pale whiskers.
sections.habitat: Muskrats use marshes, ponds, lakes, streams, drainage canals and estuarine wetlands where water and food remain available. Dense stands of cattails, bulrushes, sedges or reeds provide both edible shoots and cover, while open water lets them travel between feeding and resting sites. In Texas, shallow marshes with stable water around 15–60 cm supported especially favorable conditions; that local range should not be treated as a universal requirement. Houses of cut marsh vegetation rise above water, whereas animals along rivers and canals may excavate bank burrows with underwater entrances.
sections.diet: The diet consists mostly of aquatic plants, especially roots, rhizomes and lower stems of cattails, sedges, bulrushes and water lilies. Strong incisors cut this vegetation, and lips that close behind the incisors allow the animal to gnaw while submerged without taking water into its mouth. It often carries plant pieces to a feeding platform or shelter to eat. Animal food is occasional rather than the norm: documented items include crayfish, mussels, frogs, fish and small turtles, particularly when plant food is scarce. A large, compartmentalized cecum retains fibrous food for microbial fermentation, helping process its plant-heavy diet.
sections.behavior: Muskrats are active throughout the day but often become most active from mid-afternoon into dusk. Family members may share a lodge, but crowding and breeding-season competition can cause aggression; scent from musk glands and squeaks or squeals provide communication. In winter, animals in icy regions dig for submerged roots and may build a protective feeding shelter over a hole in the ice.
sections.reproduction: The breeding season shifts with latitude; in Indiana, most litters arrive in May and June, and females may produce two to four litters per year. After about 28–30 days of gestation, a female gives birth in a grass- or cattail-lined nest, commonly to around six kits. They are born blind and helpless, begin swimming at roughly ten days, and can eat green plants at about three weeks. The mother nurses them until weaning at three to four weeks; young may remain with her longer, especially in the final litter of the season. A two-season field study found that male care varied with mating strategy, and juvenile survival in that study did not depend on the amount of paternal care.
sections.ecology: Muskrats are prey for mink, otters, foxes, coyotes, owls, hawks and other wetland predators, linking plant production to higher trophic levels. Their grazing and the vegetation they pile into lodges or feeding platforms can open dense marsh stands into a mosaic of channels, grazed patches and emergent cover. This effect depends on local density and plant growth: heavy grazing can strip vegetation or weaken banks, while moderate activity creates structural variety. Lodges can also be used by other wetland animals as nesting or resting sites.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment completed on 20 August 2016 classified the species as Least Concern, citing its broad range and lack of major global threats; this is not a current census of every population. A 42-year analysis of harvest records from 37 U.S. states found evidence of decline from 1970 to 2012 after accounting for pelt prices, with a steeper trend in the Southeast; harvest data remain an indirect measure. The European Union’s consolidated regulation of 7 August 2025 still lists the muskrat as an invasive alien species of Union concern. It was added to that list by Commission Implementing Regulation 2017/1263 in 2017. Burrowing can damage dikes and banks, and intense grazing can alter wetlands, so European management addresses local ecological and infrastructure impacts.
